title: How your phone knows where a plane is

segments.text: How does your phone know where a plane is right now?
The plane gives itself away. It broadcasts its own position, once a second.
Step one: the plane works out where it is from GPS satellites.
Step two: a radio onboard sends that out, with its altitude, speed and ID.
Step three: receivers on the ground pick it up. Some are run by hobbyists at home.
Over the ocean, receivers on satellites can catch it too.
Flight tracking apps gather these signals and show each plane on your map.
And in the US, it's now air traffic control's preferred way to track planes.
Save this for your next flight.

sources: FAA Flight Standards, ADS-B page, https://www.faa.gov/about/office_org/headquarters_offices/avs/offices/afx/afs/afs400/afs410/ads-b : 'ADS-B Out works by broadcasting information about an aircraft's GPS location, altitude, ground speed and other data to ground stations and other aircraft, once per second.'

14 CFR 91.227(d), eCFR https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-91/subpart-C/section-91.227 : minimum broadcast message set includes latitude and longitude, barometric pressure altitude, velocity, aircraft identification (flight plan / ATC call sign) and the ICAO 24-bit address.

14 CFR 91.225, eCFR https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-91/subpart-C/section-91.225 : ADS-B Out required after January 1, 2020 in Class A airspace and (below 18,000 ft MSL) in Class B and C airspace, Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL in the 48 contiguous states (excluding at and below 2,500 ft above the surface), and other listed areas.

FAA ADS-B overview, https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/technology/adsb : 'Real-time ADS-B is now the preferred method of surveillance for air traffic control in the NAS' (NAS = U.S. National Airspace System).

FAA ADS-B FAQ, https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/technology/adsb/faq : ADS-B moves 'from ground radar and navigational aids to precise tracking using satellite signals'; ground stations are 'so much easier to place than radar'.

FlightAware ADS-B, https://www.flightaware.com/adsb/ : 'FlightAware operates a worldwide network of ADS-B and Mode S receivers'; users can 'build a Raspberry Pi with a USB ADS-B receiver' and 'feed additional ADS-B data from their receivers'; it also receives 'over 45 different government air traffic control and private datalink sources'. FlightFeeder page, https://www.flightaware.com/adsb/flightfeeder/ : receivers provided 'free of charge to qualified individuals who agree to host them' ('To volunteer to host a FlightFeeder').

Aireon, https://aireon.com/ : 'Powered by Iridium's networked constellation of 66 satellites, Aireon ADS-B provides continuous air traffic surveillance to areas of the world that previously had no access to this information, including over oceans'.
